title: Containers, Kubernetes and CI/CD for ML
oneLiner: Package the model with everything it needs (containers), run many copies reliably (Kubernetes), and ship changes automatically (CI/CD).

what.html:
A container bundles your model, code, libraries and settings so it runs the same on any machine. Docker builds and runs containers. Kubernetes runs many containers across many machines, restarting them when they fail and adding copies when traffic grows. CI/CD automatically tests, packages and deploys every change.

Everyday versionA singer whose concerts kept failing because of the venues' microphones starts bringing their own kit (containers). A tour manager decides which venues host which shows and books a replacement if one cancels (Kubernetes).

why.html:
• "It works on my machine" stops being an excuse when the machine travels with the code.
  • Real traffic needs many copies, automatic recovery and rolling updates.
  • Manual deployments are slow, error-prone and hard to undo.

how.title: From servers to orchestration
how.html: Apps on bare servers clashed; virtual machines isolated them but each needs a whole OS; containers share the OS and start in seconds; Kubernetes manages containers across a cluster. ML deployment needs packaging, serving, scaling and MLOps.

how.title: Containers vs virtual machines
how.html: A container holds code, runtime, system libraries and settings, and shares the host's kernel. A VM carries a full operating system. Containers are much lighter and faster to start; VMs isolate more strongly.

how.title: Dockerfile → image → container
how.html: A Dockerfile is the recipe (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD…). docker build turns it into an image made of layers. docker run starts a container from it; one image can run many containers. Images are shared through registries like Docker Hub.

how.title: Put a model in a box
how.html: Train, save model.pkl, write a FastAPI app.py with pre- and post-processing, list libraries in requirements.txt, build the image, run it on port 8000 and POST flower measurements to /predict. The reply: {"prediction": 0, "class": "setosa"}.

how.title: Kubernetes keeps things running
how.html: The control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) decides where things run; worker nodes (kubelet, kube-proxy) run the containers. You say "3 copies"; if one dies, a new one appears; if a node fails, its work moves elsewhere.

how.title: Pods, Deployments and YAML
how.html: A pod is one or more containers with its own IP. A Deployment, written in YAML, says which image and how many replicas; kubectl apply -f file.yaml makes it happen. Minikube runs a small cluster on a laptop for practice.

demo.html: Follow one change from a developer's push, through tests and an image registry, to a deployment repository that an agent like Argo CD syncs into the cluster. Rolling back is just reverting a Git commit.

example.html:
A fraud model at a payments company. The model and FastAPI app are packaged into an image tagged fraud:2.3.1. A Kubernetes Deployment runs 6 replicas across 3 nodes; at month-end the autoscaler raises it to 15. When a node dies at 2 am, its pods are rescheduled within seconds. A new model version goes through CI, the image tag changes in the deployment repo, and Argo CD performs a rolling update with no downtime.

Supplementary Readiness probes stop traffic reaching a pod until the model has finished loading.

misunderstandings: They share the host kernel and have no guest OS.
An image and a container are the same thing.
An image is the template; a container is a running instance.
It runs and manages containers from images built elsewhere.
Pin versions so deployments and rollbacks are exact.
takeaways: Deployment evolved: servers → VMs → containers → Kubernetes.
Containers package code, runtime, libraries and settings; they share the host kernel.
Dockerfile → image (layers) → container; registries share images.
Kubernetes: control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controllers) + workers (kubelet, kube-proxy); pods, Deployments, Services in YAML.
CI/CD with GitOps: CI builds and tests, Git declares state, Argo CD syncs the cluster.
thirty: Deployment evolved from apps on physical servers to virtual machines with their own guest OS, to containers sharing the host kernel, to Kubernetes orchestrating containers across clusters. ML deployment means serving a trained model on live data via REST or gRPC, and needs packaging, serving, scaling and MLOps. A Dockerfile, using FROM, RUN, COPY and CMD, builds a layered image, and each running copy of it is a container, so a FastAPI iris model in an image answers POST /predict anywhere. Kubernetes' control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) and worker nodes (kubelet, kube-proxy) run pods declared in YAML Deployments, keeping the desired replica count and recovering from failures. CI/CD with GitOps builds and tests images, records the desired state in a deployment repository, and lets Argo CD sync the cluster.

check.q: What do containers share that VMs don't?

check.why: A running instance of the image.

check.q: Which component stores the Kubernetes cluster state?
The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes is…
check.why: One or more containers with an IP.

check.q: In GitOps, the desired cluster state lives in…
check.why: Deployment repo; Argo CD syncs it.
